opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've been thinking about for a long time, and my view has changed quite a bit.

Early in my PhD, around the time of ResNeXt and the work before it, I was a true believer in architecture. The feeling in the field was that the network design itself was where the intelligence came from. If you found the right inductive bias, the right topology, the right way to aggregate features, you'd unlock better representations. Architecture engineering was the main game, and a lot of us spent years on it.

Then Vision Transformers came along, and that was a real moment of reflection for me. People started saying convolution was dead and attention was the key ingredient. With ConvNeXt, part of what we wanted to understand was whether that was actually true. What we found, roughly, was that if you modernize a plain ConvNet with the training recipes and macro design choices that came with Transformers, you can close most of the gap. That taught me something humbling: many of the gains we credited to architecture were really coming from data, training procedures, scale, and objectives.

So my view shifted. Architecture matters, but more as an enabler than the source of the representation. It sets how efficiently you can scale, what's easy or hard to learn, and how well you use compute. The representation itself is shaped much more by the learning signal: what data you see, what objective you optimize, what you ask the model to predict. That's partly why I became so interested in self-supervised learning, things like masked autoencoders, and later in how representations connect to generative models. Work like REPA showed that aligning a diffusion model's internal features with a strong pretrained visual encoder can make training much faster and better. That suggests representation is something shared across tasks, and not owned by any one architecture.

Today I'd put it this way: architecture is like the shape of the container, and the representation is what fills it. A bad container can definitely hurt you. But past a certain point, the more interesting questions are about what fills it. What does the model need to learn about the world? What supervision gets it there? And how do vision and language representations relate to each other? I've also become more convinced that visual representation learning is still underexplored compared to language. We may have over-indexed on language as the backbone of intelligence, and there's a lot of room to rethink what a good visual representation really is.

So I've gone from "architecture is everything" to "architecture is necessary but not sufficient," and lately to "let's focus on the learning problem and let architecture follow."

r001.rationale: The response says architecture is an enabler rather than the source of representation, and that data, training procedures, scale, and objectives account for many gains.

r002.rationale: It describes architecture as shaping what is efficient to learn, while data and the objective shape the representation, communicating their combined influence.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I've been sitting with for a long time, because my own trajectory kind of forced me to keep revising the answer.

When I started, around the ResNet and ResNeXt era, I genuinely believed architecture was the main thing. The story we told ourselves was that if you design the right inductive biases, the right wiring, the network will learn better representations. Depth, residual connections, grouped convolutions, cardinality, all of that felt like the lever. And to be fair, at that time it was. Those changes produced real, measurable jumps.

Then Transformers came, and ViT in particular, and the field basically said convolutions are over, attention is the future. I didn't fully buy that, which is partly why we did ConvNeXt. The point of ConvNeXt wasn't really that ConvNets are better. It was that when you modernize the training recipe, the data, the design details, a pure ConvNet can match a Transformer. What that taught me is that a lot of what we attributed to architecture was actually coming from the training recipe and the scale of data. The architecture was getting credit it didn't fully deserve.

So my view shifted to something like: architecture is less about what representation you learn and more about how efficiently you can learn it. Given enough data and compute, many reasonable architectures converge toward similar representations. The differences show up in scalability, in hardware friendliness, in how gracefully things degrade when you have less data. Architecture became, in my mind, an engineering question about the path rather than a scientific question about the destination.

But then I think I overcorrected, and more recently I've swung back a bit. Working on things like DiT for diffusion, and then on representation alignment, I started seeing that the representation learning objective and the architecture are not actually separable. What you optimize for shapes what you can learn, but the architecture determines what's easy to express. In generative models for example, we found that the internal representations of a diffusion Transformer can be fairly weak semantically, and if you encourage them to align with a good self-supervised encoder, the whole model trains faster and generates better. That's not an architecture story alone, and it's not an objective story alone. It's the interaction.

So where I've landed, roughly, is that architecture is a vessel. It doesn't create the representation, but it constrains it, and the constraints matter more at the boundaries, when data is limited, when you need a certain kind of structure like spatial locality or long-range dependency, when you care about compute. In the middle, in the big scale regime, the architecture matters less than people think and the data plus objective matters more. I've become much more humble about architecture and much more interested in what representations actually emerge and why, rather than in designing clever modules.

If anything, the lesson is that every few years I convince myself I understand the role of architecture, and then the field shows me I was looking at a narrow slice of the picture. I try to hold my current view loosely.

r001.rationale: The response says that at large scale architecture matters less than people think, while data and the objective matter more.

r002.rationale: It describes architecture, data scale, and training recipe as jointly shaping results, and explicitly says architecture and the learning objective interact in determining what representations emerge.

astra-6.text:
I think my view has shifted from architecture as the main driver of progress to architecture as one part of a much larger system. Earlier, I was very interested in the structure itself: how you connect layers, how you organize computation, and what inductive biases you build into the network. Those choices felt central to learning good representations.

I still think they matter, but you can’t really separate them from the data, the training objective, and the amount of compute. An architecture that looks limited under one training recipe can become very strong under another. So when we compare two architectures, we have to ask whether we’re actually measuring the architecture or the entire recipe around it.

That also changes what makes architecture research interesting to me. It’s less about finding a clever module that gives you a small improvement on a benchmark, and more about understanding which design choices make learning more efficient, more scalable, or more useful across tasks. Architecture gives the model a way to organize and process information, but the representations emerge from how that structure interacts with learning. I’ve become much more interested in that interaction.

r001.rationale: It describes architecture as one part of a larger system, rather than the main driver of progress in learning representations.

r002.rationale: It says architecture cannot be separated from the data and training objective, and that representations emerge from how the structure interacts with learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I used to think of architecture as the main driver of representation learning. You design a better network, it learns better features, and performance improves. Over time, I’ve come to see architecture as one part of a larger system: the data, the learning objective, the optimization, and the compute budget all interact with it.

That doesn’t mean architecture no longer matters. It shapes the inductive biases of the model—what kinds of patterns are easy to learn—and determines how efficiently you can train and scale it. But a comparison between two architectures can also be a comparison between their training recipes. You have to disentangle those factors before attributing an improvement to the architecture itself.

So the question I find more interesting now is: what does this architectural choice make possible? Does it improve learning efficiency? Does it scale well? Does it help representations transfer across tasks? That’s a broader view than simply asking which network gets the highest accuracy on one benchmark.

r001.rationale: The candidate says architecture is no longer the main driver and is one part of a larger system, communicating that it may not be the most important factor.

r002.rationale: The candidate explicitly says architecture, data, and the learning objective interact in representation learning.
